title: Chili Piper Chat vs Qualified: How Storylane RepX Compares (2026)
summary: Chili Piper Chat vs Qualified in 2026: pricing, routing, and Salesforce lock-in, plus how Storylane RepX closes the after-the-click gap.
body_markdown:
I'll say the quiet part first: the chili piper chat vs qualified decision in 2026 is not really a feature bake-off anymore. It is a bet on which CRM ecosystem you are willing to be locked into. Salesforce completed its acquisition of Qualified on April 1, 2026, and that single fact reshapes the whole comparison (Salesforce, 2026).


I'm Madhav Bhandari, CMO at Storylane. My take is blunt: for most non-Salesforce teams, the honest answer to "Chili Piper or Qualified?" is "neither, not this quarter." For the full landscape, see our roundup of[Chili Piper Chat alternatives](https://www.storylane.io/blog/chili-piper-chat-alternatives) .


And whichever you land on, the booked meeting is only half the job. What happens after the calendar invite fires is where deals are won or lost.


## Quick Answer: Chili Piper Chat vs Qualified at a glance


> **TL;DR:** Chili Piper is a routing and scheduling platform that works with both Salesforce and HubSpot. Qualified is a website-first conversational AI, and as of April 1, 2026 it is a Salesforce-owned product line, not an independent vendor. If you run Salesforce and want autonomous inbound engagement, Qualified is the more ambitious tool. If you run HubSpot or a multi-CRM stack, Chili Piper is the safer routing layer, and you should treat Qualified's roadmap as a Salesforce roadmap.


Neither tool, on its own, closes the loop between "visitor lands on your site" and "prospect actually understands your product." That gap is the reason this article exists.


I am not neutral here. Storylane sits in the part of the funnel both of these tools hand off to, so read the product section with that disclosed. Everything else is called as I see it, including where competitors beat us.


## Chili Piper Chat vs Qualified vs Storylane RepX: the comparison table


Here is the fast orientation before we get into the substance. The third column is Storylane, because the "after the booking" step keeps getting left out of every comparison I read, and I think that omission is the most expensive one buyers make.


The way to read this table is by job to be done. Chili Piper's job is deciding who a lead goes to and getting it on a calendar.


Qualified's job is holding an autonomous conversation on your site and qualifying the visitor in real time. Storylane's job starts a beat later, when that visitor wants to actually see the product. Those are three different problems, and most teams need at least two of them solved, which is why a single-column winner rarely exists in this category.


Category Chili Piper Qualified Storylane RepX


Core function Lead routing and meeting scheduling Website conversational AI (Piper agent) Interactive demos and an AI demo agent


CRM support Salesforce and HubSpot Salesforce (now Salesforce-owned) CRM-agnostic, works alongside either


Pricing entry point Per-seat from ~$15/user/mo plus platform fees Custom annual, no public list price Not publicly listed; request a quote


Best-fit team RevOps needing routing across CRMs Salesforce-first enterprise marketing Teams selling a product buyers want to see


Read that table as a starting map, not a verdict. The interesting decisions live in the sections below, especially the ownership change most competing pages still ignore.


## What each platform actually does


> **Definition:** A conversational engagement platform is software that turns a website visit into a real-time, qualified conversation, then routes or books the visitor into a sales motion. Chili Piper and Qualified attack that job from opposite ends.


### Chili Piper: routing and scheduling across Chat, Concierge, Distro, and Handoff


Chili Piper is, at its heart, a routing and scheduling engine. Its strength is the plumbing: matching an inbound lead to the right rep and booking a meeting without a human in the loop.


The product line covers the mechanics of that handoff:


- **Form Concierge:** qualify and book directly off an inbound web form.
- **Distro:** automated, no-code lead distribution to the right rep.
- **Handoff:** pass a meeting from one rep to another without a spreadsheet.
- **Chat:** the conversational front end that ties the routing logic to a live site.


That focus is also the limit. Chili Piper is excellent at deciding who a lead goes to and when they meet, and deliberately light on helping the visitor understand your product first.


### Qualified: website-first conversational AI, now inside Salesforce Agentforce


Qualified comes at inbound from the conversation side. Its flagship, the Piper agent, engages visitors in chat, qualifies them against CRM data, and books meetings autonomously.


Say it plainly, because most pages don't: Qualified is now a Salesforce-owned product line, not an independent vendor. Salesforce is folding it into Agentforce Sales and Agentforce Marketing (Salesforce, 2026). That reshapes[how lead qualification actually works](https://www.storylane.io/blog/the-ultimate-guide-to-sales-qualification) once your qualification logic lives inside one vendor's CRM.


## The acquisition nobody else is explaining


Every competing page I read still frames Qualified as a plucky independent startup. That framing is out of date, and it will make those pages look stale within weeks.


Here is the timeline that matters:


1. **December 17, 2025:** Salesforce signs a definitive agreement to acquire Qualified (Salesforce, 2026).
2. **April 1, 2026:** Salesforce completes the acquisition. Qualified is now part of Salesforce (Salesforce, 2026).
3. **After close:** Qualified's Piper capabilities are being folded into Agentforce Sales and Agentforce Marketing (Salesforce, 2026).


> The practical read: an independent product roadmap effectively freezes, and future development follows Salesforce's priorities, not Qualified's original ones. That is not automatically bad. If you are a Salesforce-first enterprise, deeper native integration is a real upside. If you are not, you just inherited a dependency you did not sign up for.


Own that knowledge before you sit in a demo, not after you sign. If the ownership change is a dealbreaker, weigh the[Qualified alternatives](https://www.storylane.io/blog/qualified-alternatives) before you renew.


## Why this matters if you're not on Salesforce


If your CRM is HubSpot, or you run a multi-CRM stack, the acquisition is not a footnote. It is the decision.


Qualified is built for Salesforce, and now it is owned by Salesforce. Betting your inbound conversion layer on it is a bet that you will be a Salesforce shop for the life of that contract, while Chili Piper still supports both Salesforce and HubSpot.


Before you sign anything with Qualified, get direct answers to these questions:


- Which parts of the product require Salesforce CRM as a hard prerequisite, today and on the roadmap?
- What is the committed support timeline for non-Salesforce integrations post-acquisition?
- How will packaging and pricing change as the Qualified SKU is absorbed into Agentforce?
- What is the migration path if I am on HubSpot and need to leave in two years?


One buyer we spoke with was refreshingly clear about wanting to protect the investment they had already made in routing:


"What we want most at the moment is we need a robust AI chat. We have Chili Piper right now, and we want to keep Chili Piper for the logic. Like, we have so much routing logic set up to our sales teams, and so I guess that's number one, is if we onboarded Storylane, would you guys let us keep the Chili Piper logic in place and would you integrate with that?" - \[Senior Vertical Marketing Manager, industry not captured\]


That instinct is correct: the buying question for most teams is not "rip and replace," it is "what can I add on top without losing what already works."


## The conversational marketing category is consolidating


Zoom out, because the Qualified deal is not an isolated event. The independent conversational-marketing category is being absorbed into CRM platforms at speed, and that is the real context for your decision.


Inside roughly a seven-month window:


1. **Drift:** the standalone product was set for sunset in 2026 under Salesloft, with 1mind named as the successor path (Salesloft, 2026).
2. **Qualified:** acquired by Salesforce, completed April 1, 2026 (Salesforce, 2026).
3. **Warmly:** acquired by HubSpot in June 2026 (HubSpot, 2026).
4. **Fin, formerly Intercom:** Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire it in June 2026 for roughly $3.6 billion, a deal that is signed but not yet closed (Salesforce, 2026).


The pattern is unmistakable: buyers are no longer picking a point tool, they are picking a CRM ecosystem. That reframes an[intent-based marketing strategy](https://www.storylane.io/blog/intent-based-marketing) around a platform bet, not a feature checklist, so make the bet consciously rather than backing into it through a chat vendor. It also helps to see the same decision from other angles:[Chili Piper vs Drift](https://www.storylane.io/blog/chili-piper-vs-drift) ,[Chili Piper vs Intercom](https://www.storylane.io/blog/chili-piper-vs-intercom) , and[Spara vs Chili Piper](https://www.storylane.io/blog/spara-vs-chili-piper) .


## Feature-by-feature comparison


The at-a-glance table gave you the shape. This one gives you the detail, including the channel coverage most single-vendor pages gloss over.


Read each row as a question about your own motion, not a scoreboard. If your inbound comes through forms and you live in a mature routing setup, Chili Piper's depth is the row that matters and the AI column is a bonus.


If your bet is that an autonomous agent should carry the whole conversation, Qualified's AI capability is the row to weigh, provided you are Salesforce-native enough to feed it clean data. And if the honest gap in your funnel is that visitors never see the product before a call, the implementation and channel rows point somewhere neither vendor covers.

Notice the theme. Chili Piper wins on routing depth and CRM flexibility, Qualified wins on autonomous conversation depth if you are Salesforce-native, and neither actually shows the buyer the product. Pairing routing with real[buyer intent signals](https://www.storylane.io/blog/how-to-use-purchase-intent-to-improve-your-sales) only helps if what happens next is worth the buyer's time.


## Chili Piper Chat vs Qualified: pricing and total cost of ownership


Pricing here is genuinely hard to pin down. Published figures vary source to source, and post-acquisition packaging for Qualified is a moving target.


Chili Piper starts around $15 per user per month and layers a platform fee on top for each product you switch on, so the bill scales with both headcount and how much of the suite you adopt (Chili Piper, 2026). Qualified sells custom annual contracts with no public list price, and that packaging is a moving target as its SKU is absorbed into Agentforce.


Cost element Chili Piper Qualified


List price basis Per-seat from ~$15/user/mo plus per-product platform fee Custom annual contract


Platform fees One fee per product you enable Bundled into the annual figure


Year-one cost (illustrative) Low five figures at modest seat counts Enterprise-tier, quoted per deal


A quick illustrative example, built on assumed rates rather than a quote. A 25-seat Chili Piper deployment at a blended $30 per user per month is $9,000 per year in seats, plus say $500 per month in platform fees, for roughly $15,000 in year one before discounts.


That is an order of magnitude below a typical Qualified enterprise contract, which is the honest reason smaller teams pick routing over full conversational AI. Model your own seat count and product mix rather than trusting any single published number.


## Implementation time and operational overhead


This is where the two tools diverge most. Chili Piper states a 2-3 week Chat rollout. Qualified's timeline is tied to the depth of your Salesforce integration, and in practice it runs heavier.


The overhead is not really the license, it is the build. Qualified asks you to design conversation flows and produce a lot of content, and buyers feel that. One marketing leader who had actually used it put the cost plainly:


"I've used qualified and it was a lot of work on the back end to set up the like if then flows and it but it was, you know, it was only chat based so you couldn't pull up video content." - \[Head of Marketing, industry not captured\]


That is two problems in one sentence: heavy setup, and a chat-only ceiling. Factor both into your total cost, because a tool that eats a quarter of RevOps time is expensive no matter what the invoice says. When you scope this, map it against[your broader sales tech stack](https://www.storylane.io/blog/tools-to-build-the-best-sales-tech-stack) so you are not paying twice for overlapping capabilities.


## Reviews and ratings: what real users say


Ratings alone won't decide this. On G2 in 2026, Chili Piper carries roughly a 4.6 out of 5, and Qualified sits around 4.9 out of 5 with a large review base (G2, 2026).


Signal Chili Piper Qualified


G2 rating (2026) ~4.6 / 5 ~4.9 / 5


Most-praised strength Routing and scheduling reliability Conversation quality of the AI agent


Common critique Config complexity, stacking fees Setup effort, chat-only content


Scores are the easy part. The more useful signal is how buyers describe the problem in their own words. One senior leader in higher education was blunt about the tooling they had outgrown:


"our website is in the process of being updated at the moment, but part of the journey, we use HubSpot and HubSpot's chatbot just isn't fit for purpose, never was." - \[Senior Leader, higher education\]


The same buyer described the booking flow they were living with, and why it frustrated them:


"It's typically a HubSpot calendar coming off the back of a form. So that's how we're doing it at the moment. But, you know, that doesn't work great in a lot of cases. It's a bit. There's about six steps in the process." - \[Senior Leader, higher education\]


Six steps to book a meeting is the pain both Chili Piper and Qualified promise to remove. Keep that yardstick in mind: does the tool collapse those steps, or just relabel them?


## After the meeting is booked: the step nobody compares


Full disclosure: this is us. Storylane sits in the exact gap both of these tools leave open, so weigh this section knowing that.


Neither Chili Piper nor Qualified owns what happens after the meeting is booked, or before it, when a prospect wants to see the product without talking to anyone. One CEO described the job to be done almost perfectly:


"I want to try and book meetings from the site. I also want people to watch short videos and get slide presented and things like that. Just basically speed up the sales process." - \[CEO, industry not captured\]


A marketing leader named the underlying shift in buyer behavior:


"I see the value in it especially with how little people want to interact with you or your sales team before they actually book a call." - \[Head of Marketing, industry not captured\]


Pair either routing tool with an interactive product demo, a Storylane-style guided walkthrough, and a visitor can experience the product first, self-qualify, and arrive at the booked meeting already convinced. Storylane RepX adds an AI demo agent that can answer product questions inside that walkthrough, and it is a practical way of[converting demo requests](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-requests) into pipeline. If you are also evaluating autonomous agents on both ends of the funnel, our guide to the[best AI SDR tools](https://www.storylane.io/blog/best-ai-sdr-tools) puts these categories side by side.


Where does Storylane not fit? If your problem is purely "route this lead to the right rep and get it on a calendar," we are not your tool, Chili Piper is. We earn our place after the click.


## Which should you choose?


The decision comes down to your CRM, your appetite for lock-in, and how much of the product story the buyer experiences before a call. That last part is where an[enterprise sales software stack](https://www.storylane.io/blog/enterprise-sales-software) either compounds or leaks.


- **Choose Chili Piper if** you need mature, flexible routing across Salesforce and HubSpot, you want a fast rollout, and conversational AI is a nice-to-have rather than the point.
- **Choose Qualified if** you are Salesforce-first, you want an autonomous inbound AI agent, and you are comfortable that its roadmap is now Salesforce's roadmap.
- **Choose neither yet if** you are CRM-agnostic and risk-averse right now, because the category is consolidating fast and locking into a chat vendor mid-shake-out is the one move you cannot easily undo.


Whichever way you go on chili piper chat vs qualified, solve the after-the-click gap deliberately. The routing tool that wins you the meeting still needs something worth showing.

## FAQ


**Is Qualified still an independent company?**


No. Salesforce completed its acquisition of Qualified on April 1, 2026, and it is now a Salesforce-owned product line being folded into Agentforce. Treat its roadmap as a Salesforce roadmap.


**What happens to my Qualified contract now that Salesforce owns it?**


Existing contracts generally continue, but packaging and pricing can change as the SKU is absorbed into Agentforce. Ask your rep in writing for the committed support timeline on non-Salesforce integrations before you renew.


**Does Chili Piper work with HubSpot?**


Yes. Chili Piper supports both Salesforce and HubSpot, a meaningful advantage if you are not a Salesforce shop. Qualified is built for Salesforce and is now owned by Salesforce.


**Which is faster to implement, Chili Piper or Qualified?**


Chili Piper states a 2-3 week Chat rollout, while Qualified's timeline tracks the depth of your Salesforce integration and runs heavier. The bigger cost with Qualified is building conversation flows and content, not the license.


**Do I still need an interactive demo if I use one of these tools?**


Usually yes. Both tools get a meeting booked, but neither lets a prospect experience your product before or after the call, and that self-serve step is increasingly what buyers want.
